entries.name: Quartz sand
entries.notes: The common case: beach and dune sand is mostly quartz grains. One block ≈ dry or wet sand; depth below a beach or dune is a few metres before sandstone.

entries.name: Silt
entries.notes: Finer than sand, coarser than clay (0.002-0.063 mm). River mud; the Nile delta owes its fertility to it.

entries.name: Loam
entries.notes: The balanced farmer's soil: roughly equal parts sand, silt and clay plus humus. Density given is bulk (loose), not grain.

entries.name: Kaolin (china clay)
entries.weathers_to: kaolinite residue; erodes into ball-clay seams
entries.notes: The white pottery clay. Kaolinized granite is soft enough to crumble under a shovel; the geology is unmistakable.

entries.name: Kaolinite
entries.notes: The reference clay mineral: soft, white, non-swelling, low plasticity. Most porcelain and most paper coating starts here.

entries.name: Bentonite
entries.notes: A smectite clay that swells to many times its dry volume when wet; a few centimetres seal a pond. Sodium bentonite is the common grade.

entries.name: Ball clay
entries.notes: Highly plastic secondary kaolin-family clay; 'ball' from the lumps dug in Devon and shipped as balls. Adds workability to lean kaolin bodies.

entries.name: Fire clay
entries.notes: Kaolinite-rich clay that survives kiln and furnace heat (over 1500 C softening); mined deep because the best grades lie under coal measures.

entries.name: Illite
entries.notes: The dominant clay in shales and the end product of smectite aging in the burial window; most 'plain clay' is mostly illite.

entries.name: Montmorillonite
entries.notes: The swelling member of the smectite family; cracked, gilgai-patterned vertisol soils are its signature on the surface.

entries.name: Shale
entries.notes: Compacted, fissile clay rock; splits into thin sheets. Black shales are the source of most shale-gas plays.

entries.name: Loess
entries.notes: Wind-blown silt laid down in vast blankets; it stands in vertical cliffs and caves are hand-dug into it. The Chinese Loess Plateau is the type example.

entries.name: Laterite
uses: building brick (cut wet, hardens in air)
entries.notes: The deep-red rusted regolith of the wet tropics; cut while soft it bakes in the sun into a workable building block.

entries.name: Silica sand
found: glass-sand districts (e.g. high-purity US and Belgian pits)
entries.notes: High-purity quartz sand, washed and graded to spec; the difference from beach sand is glass-making purity, not species.

entries.name: Claystone
entries.notes: Mud rock that no longer splits into sheets; the massive, blocky cousin of shale. Quarried for brick in many countries.

entries.name: Mudstone
entries.notes: Any hardened mud: silt plus clay, no fissility required. The general term when shale and claystone are too specific.

entries.name: Marl
entries.notes: Half clay, half limestone mud; farmers dug and spread it on acid soils for centuries to sweeten them.

entries.name: Diatomite (diatomaceous earth)
entries.notes: A rock that is mostly fossilized diatom shells; solid density is high but the rock is mostly pores (bulk density can be under 1000). Famous as the filler in Alfred Nobel's dynamite.

entries.name: Terra rossa
entries.notes: The red soil sitting as pockets in dissolving limestone; the signature soil of the Mediterranean and of the Coonawarra wine belt.

entries.name: Fuller's earth
entries.notes: Named for fullers, who kneaded it into raw wool to strip out grease before felting; chemically it is attapulgite or smectite earth.

entries.name: Coral sand
entries.notes: Sand ground from reef life: shell, coral and coralline algae. It fizzes in weak acid and keeps tropical lagoons clear and white.

entries.name: Volcanic sand
entries.notes: Freshly ground black lava; iron-rich, dense and quickly turned into extraordinarily fertile soil. Retains little water but grows lush crops.

entries.name: Black sand
entries.notes: The heavy streak where waves winnow out the quartz; a dark line on the tide line. Often radioactive if monazite is present.

entries.name: Greensand (glauconite)
uses: greensand historically used to filter town water
entries.notes: Dark green, potassium-bearing marine sand that glistens faintly; farmers dug 'greensand marl' onto fields for potash before mined fertilizers.

entries.name: Gypsum sand
entries.notes: A whole desert of pure white sand that is not quartz at all: the White Sands dunes are gypsum ground by wave action, unique because gypsum sand dunes almost never survive elsewhere.

entries.name: Vermiculite
entries.notes: Flakes that puff up 8-30x into golden worm-like coils when heated to ~1000 C; the classic attic insulation of mid-century houses.

entries.name: Halloysite
entries.notes: Kaolinite that rolled itself into tiny hollow tubes; draws the same white color as kaolin but with tubular, lumened particles.

entries.name: Chlorite
entries.notes: The deep-green 'green clay' of metamorphic rocks; its presence marks low-grade metamorphism. Common in the clay fraction of temperate soils.

entries.name: Palygorskite (attapulgite)
entries.notes: A fibrous clay that gels even in seawater; chemically the core of the famous pre-Columbian Maya blue pigment. Long fibers may be a mesothelioma hazard (IARC 2B).

entries.name: Sepiolite
entries.notes: Known as meerschaum: soft, white, porous and carves beautifully; pipe bowls of meerschaum darken gradually to a cherry-brown with use.

entries.name: Feldspathic sand (arkosic sand)
found: fanglomerates and alluvial fans near mountains
entries.weathers_to: arkose rock; chemically mature residue of quartz sand and kaolin
uses: china clay feedstock (the parent of kaolin)
entries.notes: Young, immature sand right off the mountains: quartz plus unweathered feldspar. Its kaolinization in place is how kaolin deposits form.

entries.name: Olivine sand
entries.notes: One of only a handful of green beaches on Earth; the green grains are ground out of nearby dunite. Weathers fast to rust-colored iddingsite.

entries.name: Garnet sand
entries.notes: The premium blasting abrasive: hard, angular, dense and reusable. The dark-red grains litter the strandline at garnet-placer beaches.

entries.name: Zircon sand
found: beach heavy-mineral placers (Australia, South Africa, India)
entries.weathers_to: persists (extremely stable, survives everything short of melting)
entries.notes: The survivor: zircon grains are among the oldest dated materials on Earth (4.4 billion years, Jack Hills). Beach 'mineral sands' are mined for it.

entries.name: Quicksand
entries.notes: Not a place you sink forever into: a liquefied sand-water pocket that grabs a leg when disturbed. Density is bulk, water-saturated; buoyancy usually holds a swimmer up.
